La fin de semaine, à midi, le square Cab: On weekends, at noon, Cabot Square comes alive for the lunch hour. For the past few weeks, citizens have been mobilizing there every Saturday and Sunday to hand out about a hundred meals to the homeless population that gathers there.
À deux pas du square, trois fois par jou: A stone’s throw from the square, three times a day from Monday to Friday, Résilience Montréal serves 300 meals to people in need. When the COVID-19 pandemic curtailed the shelter’s activities, it was the City of Montréal that took over meal distribution. The organization was able to resume service on August 31, but is not yet able to open its doors on weekends. “We can only admit a total of 60 people in our premises, so it’s had a big impact on our activities,” says Nakuset, the executive director of Résilience Montréal.
Le foyer prend toutes les précautions de: The shelter has been taking every precaution since the start of the pandemic’s second wave and hopes to be able to open seven days a week soon. “The shelter is closed on weekends because the staff are exhausted; they needed time off,” she says. “I was afraid that if we were closed on weekends, people would have no food. So I contacted Diane Gervais, who managed to move mountains.”
Pour assurer la distribution de repas le: To ensure meals are handed out on Saturdays and Sundays, Ms. Gervais answered Nakuset’s call with the help of a friend, Kelly Warren, and Anastasia Ericson and Rose-Elizabeth Cormier, two young citizens she met online in a community group. Since September, the two have been rallying to collect donations and ensure weekend food distribution at Cabot Square.
Le groupe a aussi pu obtenir l’aide de b: The group also got help from volunteers with Khalsa Aid Canada, an international Sikh organization that teams up with the Cabot Square brigade and takes care of preparing the meals. “Even though our organization is founded on the Sikh faith, we are ready to serve anyone, regardless of religion, gender or origin,” one of the Khalsa Aid volunteers is quick to point out. When the team shows up at the meeting spot, greetings ring out.
« Tout va très bien, il n’y a eu aucun i: “Everything is going very well, there hasn’t been a single incident,” says Diane Gervais. “People are very patient, they eat and talk together.” For several decades, Cabot Square has been a gathering place for Indigenous peoples, particularly the Inuit community.
« On parle de décolonisation, mais rien: “We talk about decolonization, but nothing is being done for Cabot Square,” laments Anastasia Ericson. Dozens of homeless people can be found there every day.
<strong>Un manque de ressources aggravé: A shortage of resources made worse by COVID-19
Avec la pandémie, les services aux sans-: With the pandemic, services for people experiencing homelessness must constantly adapt to new challenges. The same goes for the citizen initiative at Cabot Square: food supplies are starting to run short, even as more and more people show up there for food on weekends. According to some people who were there, there is no similar initiative anywhere else on Saturdays and Sundays.
Nakuset indique que la Ville assurait la: Nakuset says the City used to handle food distribution in temporary outdoor shelters, including at Place Émilie-Gamelin and Place du Canada. Those operations ended on August 31. Asked about this, the City of Montréal responded that outdoor food distribution sites, like the one at Cabot Square, were opened to fill in for organizations whose services had been reduced because of the pandemic.
Ces sites fixes de distribution alimenta: These fixed food distribution sites were closed on August 31 when food aid organizations resumed their activities. The service has since gone back to the organizations. While Résilience Montréal has been able to reopen its doors, it still has to contend with the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, which prevents it from operating at full capacity. Ms. Gervais believes the City should do more. “I’m happy to help Résilience, but we shouldn’t be doing the City’s job. If Résilience lacks resources, then the City has to step in,” she argues. Nakuset points out that there is a great need for food, but also for shelter.
« Le fait que des gens se trouvent sous: “The fact that people are living under Highway 720 shows clearly that they have nowhere to go,” she insists. Last Monday morning, the encampment located not far from Atwater Avenue, near Cabot Square, was dismantled. “What are we offering to keep people warm and to feed them? What is the alternative? That’s the question I’m asking the City,” she continues, noting that shelters can only be filled to 60 per cent of their capacity because of the pandemic and the need for physical distancing. For the same reason, shopping centres, the metro and the city’s underground spaces are currently inaccessible.
À mesure que les températures baissent,: As temperatures drop, the needs of the homeless population are becoming more and more pressing. David Chapman, Résilience’s coordinator, is worried about the arrival of winter and the effects of the pandemic. He wonders where people will be able to go this year. “Among the people we serve, many can’t get into shelters at night. Last year, many used ‘in-between’ services, like a 24-hour restaurant or the metro, but that’s no longer possible this year,” he says.
Songeant à ce problème, M. Chapman crain: Thinking about this problem, Mr. Chapman fears seeing even more memorial services, after two ceremonies were held last week at Cabot Square. Before joining Résilience, the social worker worked for the organization Open Door.
À la suite du déménagement forcé du foye: After the shelter was forced to relocate to another neighbourhood, 14 deaths occurred near the square. “When you take away basic services, there are human consequences,” he says. He acknowledges that several initiatives led by the City and local authorities emerged near Cabot Square following these tragedies. “We need services for the homeless in the neighbourhood,” he insists. “If only we could have learned this lesson without people dying.”
David Chapman travaille au square Cabot: David Chapman works at Cabot Square from Monday to Friday, walkie-talkie in hand. “It’s like an extension of my family,” he says of the people who frequent the park. A large share of them, whom he estimates to be 40 per cent Inuit, come to receive the shelter’s services. Mr. Chapman adds that the City of Montréal plans to open an emergency centre for people struggling with addiction, but that he has no more information about it for now. “I know we should be able to offer about 400 beds in the city, but we don’t know when or where.”
Ces détails sont essentiels, car, selon: These details are essential because, according to him, they will determine who will be able to benefit from this service. He notes that last year, many Résilience clients were able to access the homeless services offered at the former Royal Victoria Hospital, until those suddenly changed and became a transitional housing program.
L’intervenant croit que ce type de progr: He believes this type of program, whose results are easily measurable, more readily secures funding from the very limited funds available, and that many initiatives are adapting accordingly. “It’s a good thing for the people who are admitted to this program, but the most vulnerable individuals who went to the Royal Victoria last year are wondering where they will go this year.”
La Ville de Montréal soutient qu’en répo: The City of Montréal maintains that, in response to the partial resumption of traditional emergency shelter services and the closure of temporary resources, it has implemented a transition plan that consists of ensuring beds until March 2021. “Everyone who was housed in temporary sites that closed was directed by the health network and community organizations to other shelters. No one was left behind,” we were told.
M. Chapman soutient qu’il faut des refug: Mr. Chapman maintains that shelters need to be accessible, meaning open to everyone: people who are intoxicated, people with pets, and couples. Other factors can also discourage people from going, such as having to show identification, answer questions or fill out long forms. “These are barriers for the homeless population, especially for those struggling with mental health problems,” he says.
Selon lui, un programme d’hébergement tr: In his view, a transitional housing program can be beneficial for some individuals but not for others, which creates divisions. “Those who know how to show they’re transitioning qualify, and those who can’t are still out there, in the park,” he sums up. “And it’s not for lack of willingness,” he adds. Mr. Chapman knows the stories and needs of those who frequent Cabot Square. He believes they need services better suited to the trauma they have lived through. “We live in a country that has gone through more than 100 years of cultural genocide; the legacy of all that can be seen here, in this park.”
Résilience Montréal s’occupe de tous ceu: Résilience Montréal looks after everyone who needs help. “We meet people where they are, and we respond to their needs,” Mr. Chapman explains further. “Instead of drawing up a list of the services we offer people, we ask them what they need and we help them get it.”
Le foyer offre ainsi du soutien aux toxi: The shelter thus provides support to people with substance use issues, helps some return to their northern home communities and enables others to access housing. The day centre has, among other things, a rest area, a laundry room and a shower, and offers the services of its outreach workers.
Si vous voulez faire des dons, Résilienc: If you would like to donate, Résilience Montréal is currently in need of warm clothing, new underwear, shoes, winter boots and umbrellas. Donations can be dropped off from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., Monday to Friday, at 4000 Sainte-Catherine West.
